articles.title: Heading Home: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 Concludes Station Science Mission
articles.summary: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission is ending, with the crew scheduled to return in early October. articles.content:
NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission is ending, with the crew scheduled to return in early October. NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev will head home from the International Space Station after supporting research that benefits life on Earth and prepares humans for missions into deep space.

Here’s a look back at some of their accomplishments:

Orbital transit

The crew members look out the window of a Dragon spacecraft during their journey to the space station, a destination that offers a unique vantage point to observe both Earth and the cosmos. Research in microgravity allows the scientific community to experiment through a new perspective, from changes in how cells behave to how materials take shape, space offers new paths to scientific discovery.

Learn more about research in microgravity.

Crystalline clues

NASA/Jessica Meir

Hathaway floats alongside hardware used for crystal growth experiments aboard the orbiting laboratory. Microgravity reveals new details about crystal structures, helping researchers improve the quality and stability of pharmaceuticals. Here, cancer-targeting treatments are crystallized to better understand their properties and help advance cancer therapies on Earth.

Learn more about the Pharmaceutical In-space Laboratory (ADSEP-PIL-15).

Boosting quantum science

NASA/Jack Hathaway

Meir works with cables that deliver light used to cool, trap, and study atoms inside the Cold Atom Lab. In microgravity, ultracold atoms can be observed for longer periods, giving scientists a window to peer into the quantum realm. A recent upgrade to the facility increases the number of atoms produced, providing more data to advance quantum technologies such as solar cells and the components that power cell phones and computers.

Learn more about the Cold Atom Lab.

Branching beyond bone loss

ESA/Sophie Adenot

Adenot holds a small container that houses a bone scaffold made from wood, designed to mimic the structure of real bones and support the growth of bone cells. Since microgravity can accelerate bone loss, it offers a unique opportunity to test how well the scaffold promotes bone regeneration. Insights from this study could protect future space explorers and provide new treatment options for patients with osteoporosis, a disease that affects more than 200 million people globally.

Learn more about Green Bone.

In-space suspension

NASA

Meir sets up hardware for an investigation that studies soft materials made from tiny particles suspended in water. In microgravity, scientists can study how these particles interact and assemble into structures differently than they do on Earth. Understanding these interactions could help scientists fine-tune the texture, stability, and performance of materials used for growing plants, 3D printing, and producing pharmaceuticals.

Learn more about Colloidal Solids.

Decoding microbial secrets

NASA/Jessica Meir

Hathaway holds equipment to test for antibiotic-resistant bacteria aboard the space station. Some bacteria can withstand antibiotics, starvation, and disinfection, making them a concern in closed environments like spacecraft. Sequencing DNA in microgravity can reveal how resilient microbes adapt to space, helping scientists identify countermeasures to manage antibiotic‑resistant bacteria during exploration missions while also advancing efforts to combat resistance on Earth.

Learn more about CS-05A: Genomic Enumeration of Antibiotic Resistance in Space (GEARS).

Fresh delivery

NASA/Chris Williams

Expedition 74 crew members smile among fresh produce delivered aboard NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 24 mission. Cargo flights bring critical supplies, fresh food, sweet treats, and new science to the space station. The Cygnus XL spacecraft also delivered many research projects, including an instrument that could improve space-weather modeling and a project that could help protect gut-microbiome stability on future exploration missions.

Reshaping cartilage

NASA

Meir works on an investigation that studies how engineered cartilage tissue develops in microgravity, which may help scientists produce medical implants that more closely resemble natural cartilage. For millions of people with cartilage injuries, space-grown tissue could offer treatment options that don’t require transplanting cartilage from another part of the body.

Learn more about Biomimetic Tissue Engineering in Microgravity for Cartilage using Aggregate Rejuvenation, Tension, and Self-Assembly (BEM-CARTS).

Printing meets metal

NASA

Adenot installs the Metal 3D Printer aboard the orbital complex. Several small metal parts have already been 3D printed in microgravity and returned to Earth, where their quality is evaluated against those made on the ground. Producing metal parts on demand in space could give future crews the ability to make or replace what they need far from Earth, reducing reliance on spare parts and resupply missions.

Learn more about Metal 3D Printer.

Vital fluids

NASA/Jessica Meir

Adenot works to produce intravenous (IV) fluid on demand in microgravity. Commercial IV fluids expire after about 16 months and carrying them on long-duration missions adds weight and takes up valuable space. This system could provide a critical medical resource when resupply is limited and improve access in remote areas or during emergencies on Earth.

Learn more about Intravenous Fluid Generation – Mini (IVGEN Mini).

Multiplying stem cells

NASA

Hathaway takes a selfie as Meir conducts a stem cell investigation in space. Microgravity can help produce larger numbers of clinical-grade stem cells that retain their ability to transform into other cells. Cells used in this experiment could help rebuild blood and immune systems after chemotherapy, advancing care for leukemia and other blood diseases on Earth.

Learn more about the Hematopoietic Stem Cell Expansion in Space: Pathfinder Investigation (InSPA-StemCellEX-H2).

Training bone cells

NASA/Jack Hathaway

Hathaway holds an experiment container that uses bone marrow cells to study how microgravity affects bone and muscle. The research uses structures that mimic parts of bone marrow, and some samples are exposed to vibrations that simulate exercise. Tracking changes in these cells could reveal new ways to combat bone and muscle loss during spaceflight and support bone health on Earth.

Learn more about 3D Bone Marrow Analog.

articles.personality_title: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 returns after successful space science mission
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission involved astronauts living and working on the International Space Station (ISS). The crew included NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Russian cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev. Their mission focused on scientific experiments that take advantage of the unique conditions in space.

**What happened** – The Crew-12 team is scheduled to return to Earth in early October after months in orbit. During their time on the ISS, they conducted many experiments studying everything from crystal growth and bone health to quantum science and 3D printing. These experiments used the weightless environment of space to explore things that can’t be studied the same way on Earth.

**Impact** – The research carried out by Crew-12 has practical uses on Earth and for future space travel. For example, studying crystals in space helps improve cancer medicines. Testing bone scaffolds can lead to better treatments for osteoporosis, a disease affecting millions. Experiments on stem cells and cartilage growth could improve medical treatments. Also, making metal parts and medical fluids in space could help future astronauts stay healthy and fix equipment far from Earth.

**What's next step** – After returning, scientists will analyze the data and samples brought back by the crew. The results will guide new studies and help develop better medicines and technologies. Meanwhile, NASA continues preparing for longer space missions, using what they learned to keep astronauts safe and healthy on trips to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s Crew-12 mission successfully used space conditions to advance important science that benefits health, technology, and future space exploration.
articles.personality_title_fr: La mission Crew-12 de SpaceX de la NASA revient après un succès scientifique en orbite
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La mission Crew-12 de la NASA avec SpaceX a envoyé des astronautes vivre et travailler sur la Station spatiale internationale (ISS). L’équipage comprenait Jessica Meir et Jack Hathaway de la NASA, Sophie Adenot de l’Agence spatiale européenne et le cosmonaute russe Andrey Fedyaev. Leur mission portait sur des expériences scientifiques profitant des conditions uniques de l’espace.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – L’équipage de Crew-12 doit revenir sur Terre début octobre après plusieurs mois en orbite. Pendant leur séjour à bord de l’ISS, ils ont réalisé de nombreuses expériences sur la croissance des cristaux, la santé des os, la physique quantique et l’impression 3D. Ces expériences utilisent l’absence de gravité pour étudier des phénomènes impossibles à observer de la même façon sur Terre.

**Impact** – Les recherches menées ont des applications concrètes sur Terre et pour les futurs voyages spatiaux. Par exemple, l’étude des cristaux en microgravité permet d’améliorer des médicaments contre le cancer. Tester des supports pour os peut conduire à de meilleurs traitements contre l’ostéoporose, maladie qui touche des millions de personnes. Les expériences sur les cellules souches et la croissance du cartilage pourraient améliorer les soins médicaux. De plus, fabriquer des pièces métalliques et des fluides médicaux en espace aidera les astronautes à rester en bonne santé et à réparer leur matériel loin de la Terre.

**Étape suivante** – Après leur retour, les scientifiques analyseront les données et échantillons rapportés par l’équipage. Ces résultats guideront de nouvelles études et permettront de développer de meilleurs médicaments et technologies. Pendant ce temps, la NASA prépare des missions plus longues, en utilisant ces connaissances pour protéger les astronautes lors de voyages vers la Lune, Mars et au-delà.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La mission Crew-12 de la NASA a utilisé avec succès les conditions de l’espace pour faire progresser des sciences importantes qui profitent à la santé, à la technologie et à l’exploration spatiale future.
articles.personality_title_es: La misión Crew-12 de SpaceX de la NASA regresa tras exitosa investigación en el espacio
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La misión Crew-12 de la NASA con SpaceX envió astronautas a vivir y trabajar en la Estación Espacial Internacional (EEI). La tripulación incluía a los astronautas de la NASA Jessica Meir y Jack Hathaway, la astronauta de la Agencia Espacial Europea Sophie Adenot, y el cosmonauta ruso Andrey Fedyaev. Su misión se centró en experimentos científicos que aprovechan las condiciones únicas del espacio.

**Qué pasó** – La tripulación de Crew-12 regresará a la Tierra a principios de octubre tras varios meses en órbita. Durante su estancia en la EEI, realizaron muchos experimentos sobre crecimiento de cristales, salud ósea, física cuántica e impresión 3D. Estas pruebas usan la ausencia de gravedad para estudiar cosas que no pueden observarse igual en la Tierra.

**Impacto** – La investigación realizada tiene usos prácticos en la Tierra y para futuros viajes espaciales. Por ejemplo, estudiar cristales en el espacio ayuda a mejorar medicamentos contra el cáncer. Probar andamios óseos puede llevar a mejores tratamientos para la osteoporosis, que afecta a millones. Los experimentos con células madre y crecimiento de cartílago podrían mejorar tratamientos médicos. Además, fabricar piezas metálicas y fluidos médicos en el espacio ayudará a los astronautas a mantenerse saludables y reparar equipos lejos de la Tierra.

**Próximo paso** – Tras regresar, los científicos analizarán los datos y muestras traídas por la tripulación. Los resultados guiarán nuevos estudios y ayudarán a desarrollar mejores medicinas y tecnologías. Mientras tanto, la NASA sigue preparando misiones más largas, usando lo aprendido para cuidar a los astronautas en viajes a la Luna, Marte y más allá.

**Frase clave** – La misión Crew-12 de la NASA usó con éxito las condiciones del espacio para avanzar en ciencias importantes que benefician la salud, la tecnología y la exploración espacial futura.
